newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel welcomes Primakov message from Arab states.
newsitem.headline: Israel welcomes Primakov message from Arab states.

text.p: Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said he received important information on Thursday from Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov who arrived from neighbouring Arab states.
"I was able to receive impressions and very important information from his visit to our neighbouring countries," Levy told a joint news conference after they met.
Levy declined to elaborate and it was unclear which Arab countries he was talking about. Primakov arrived in Jerusalem after holding talks with Syrian, Lebanese and Egyptian leaders.
A Syrian redeployment of some 12,000 troops in Lebanon to within striking distance of a key Israeli position on the Golan Heights had given Israelis war jitters in September.
Asked if the situation with Damascus had calmed down, Levy said: "We are working on this matter."
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday welcomed Syria's declaration this week it had no intentions of starting a war with the Jewish state.
Five years of peace talks between the two countries are stuck over the fate of the Golan Heights, captured by Israel from Syria in the 1967 Middle East war.
Primakov's visit was overshadowed in Israel by a political row over a meeting that an Israeli peacemaker, Major-General Oren Shahor, had with opposition leader Shimon Peres.

The newspaper Maariv published a front-page photo showing the officer leaving the Tel Aviv home of Peres. It said Shahor had met Peres three times in the last two months and also former Labour cabinet minister Yossi Beilin.

Right-wingers quickly took aim at the general, engaged in protracted talks with the PLO on behalf of Netanyahu's government on civilian issues linked to a long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.

"If the point of these meetings is passing secret information without prior authorisation, without the knowledge of the defence minister, it's prohibited," said Uzi Landau, a top parliament member from the ruling Likud party.
A spokesman for Shahor said the meetings were merely social calls and had no connection to peace talks.
"Only in a fascist country could such a headline top a newspaper," Beilin said.

Shahor had been a peace negotiator under Peres, Israel's prime minister until Netanyahu ousted him in elections in May. An Israeli spokeswoman said Netanyahu did not know about the meetings and promised a response later.

The affair underscored the traditionally close relations between Israel's political leaders and its generals and highlighted reported disputes between Netanyahu and Shahor over peace moves -- charges officially denied.

Primakov said he welcomed Levy's recommitment to stick to agreements Israel signed with the Arabs. In Egypt on Wednesday, he had warned Israel it risked an outburst of violence if it tried to renegotiate peace deals.

For more than three weeks Israel and the Palestinians have tried to salvage the peace process snagged on Hebron. Israel demands security guarantees for the 400 Jews who live and study in the centre of the town among 100,000 Arabs.
An Israeli spokesman said Israeli-PLO contacts were underway but it was unclear if talks would take place on Thursday.

Primakov -- whose country was a co-sponsor of the 1991 Madrid peace summit that launched Arab-Israeli peace talks -- signed an agreement with Levy transferring former Soviet property in Israel to Russia.
He was due to meet Netanyahu later on Thursday and to see Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in self-ruled Gaza on Friday. He was also due to travel to Jordan.
